      <title>Guinea-Bissau denies it has approved controversial vaccine trial in newborns</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/14/guinea-bissau-vaccine-hepatitis-b-trial-denial</link>
      <description><p>Health minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK Jr</p><p>Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday.</p><p>The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/14/guinea-bissau-vaccine-hepatitis-b-trial-denial">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding</p><p>Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).</p><p>As a result of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/sep/26/what-is-el-nino-causes-can-we-reduce-risks">the strong El Niño</a>, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/09/isaias-strengthens-first-atlantic-hurricane-2026">Continue reading...</a></description>

News from the US, Europe, Asia Pacific, Africa, Middle East, America</description><link>https://www.france24.com/en/</link><lastBuildDate>Wed, 14 Oct 2026 13:07:42 GMT</lastBuildDate><atom:link href="https://www.france24.com/en/rss" rel="self" type="application/rss+xml"/><item><category>Entre Nous</category><title>French MPs back bill to tackle sexual and gender-based violence</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/entre-nous/20261014-french-mps-back-bill-to-tackle-sexual-and-gender-based-violence</link><description>
In France, a child is reportedly raped or sexually assaulted every three minutes. In a bid to put an end to sexual and gender-based violence, French MPs have voted for a comprehensive bill that could turn into law by the end of the year; it has yet to be debated by the more conservative Senate at the end of the month. FRANCE 24's Aurore Dupuis, who made the documentary "Broken children", tells us how this new law could help improve the situation for women and children in France.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/395c39c8-c7cb-11f1-b84d-e362370cce2e/w:1024/p:16x9/capture-9b65934f.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/395c39c8-c7cb-11f1-b84d-e362370cce2e/w:1024/p:16x9/capture-9b65934f.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">3871301e-c7ca-11f1-b7e5-35bc71ba3dfb</guid><pubDate>Wed, 14 Oct 2026 12:58:52 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>Aurore Cloé DUPUIS</dc:creator></item><item><category>Asia / Pacific</category><title>Cheap weapons, growing fears: Inside the Taliban’s drone campaign against Pakistan</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/asia-pacific/20261014-taliban-suicide-drone-attacks-pakistan</link><description>
Pakistan says it intercepted 23 suicide drones launched from Afghanistan into Pakistani airspace in September alone. Since the conflict began in February 2026, the Taliban have increasingly used drones to attack Pakistan, raising concerns in Islamabad.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/5f545c36-c7b3-11f1-a790-29a2e29ae696/w:1024/p:16x9/Taliban-drones.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/5f545c36-c7b3-11f1-a790-29a2e29ae696/w:1024/p:16x9/Taliban-drones.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">864651f8-c7b5-11f1-9790-cf719f7bbb72</guid><pubDate>Wed, 14 Oct 2026 12:52:44 GMT</pubDate><source url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/5f545c36-c7b3-11f1-a790-29a2e29ae696/w:1024/p:16x9/Taliban-drones.jpg">© Observers</source><dc:creator>Ershad ALIJANI</dc:creator></item><item><category>Perspective</category><title>Trump's crackdown on migrants: New documentary investigates ICE operations</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/tv-shows/perspective/20261014-trump-s-crackdown-on-migrants-new-documentary-investigates-ice-operations</link><description>
A new documentary from our sister channel France Télévisions explores US President Donald Trump's relentless crackdown on immigration and the agency carrying it out – United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement, better known as ICE. "ICE : La chasse a l'homme", or "A Manhunt Named ICE" interviews agents and also some of the people who lives have been turned upside down by ICE operations. In Perspective, we spoke to the film's co-writer Marine Pradel.
</description><media:thumbnail url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/cb04a458-c7c3-11f1-b005-77317c09f325/w:1024/p:16x9/capture-a644f8e7.jpg"/><enclosure url="https://s.france24.com/media/display/cb04a458-c7c3-11f1-b005-77317c09f325/w:1024/p:16x9/capture-a644f8e7.jpg" type="image/jpeg" length="0"/><guid isPermaLink="false">730279f8-c7a8-11f1-9327-bd60bba74d1a</guid><pubDate>Wed, 14 Oct 2026 11:51:29 GMT</pubDate><dc:creator>Oliver FARRY</dc:creator></item><item><category>France</category><title>French student protesters are being 'exploited' by political forces, Macron says</title><link>https://www.france24.com/en/france/20261014-macron-says-french-student-protesters-exploited-by-political-forces</link><description>
French President Emmanuel Macron said on Wednesday that France's student protesters are being "exploited" by political forces ahead of the country's presidential election in April 2027. <![CDATA[ Latest from Space.com ]]> https://www.space.com/feeds.xml Wed, 14 Oct 2026 13:00:00 +0000 en <![CDATA[ The 1st SpaceX Starship to survive a launch to space just came home to its launch site ]]>

Nearly three months after surviving its launch to space and a tumultuous trial at sea, the first Starship spacecraft to survive its ocean splashdown has returned to Starbase.

SpaceX shared new photos and video of Ship 40, the Starship upper stage that launched on the developing vehicle's 13th flight test, as it completed the final stretch of its journey back to the company's South Texas facility. Now, the towering spacecraft is upright inside Starbase's Megabay hangar alongside a trio of its successor spacecraft, themselves bound for space, but not before an evaluation of Ship 40 can lend SpaceX engineers some valuable insights.

Ship 40 is the first Starship upper stage to return to its launch site after flying in space, offering SpaceX engineers an unprecedented opportunity to study hardware that survived the intense conditions of atmospheric reentry. "It will provide first-of-its-kind data on a flown Starship heatshield, Raptor engines, avionics, and more," SpaceX wrote in a post on X Oct. 13.

The spacecraft launched atop SpaceX's Super Heavy Booster 20 on July 24, and completed a suborbital flight that ended with a controlled splashdown in the Indian Ocean. Unlike previous Ship splashdowns, though, which have exploded after tipping over into the water, Ship 40 remained largely intact and afloat.

That unexpected survival prompted SpaceX to engage in an ambitious recovery effort that included towing the 171-foot (52 meter) stage though rough seas over the course of 24 days. At the time, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk expressed doubts that the company's recovery efforts would be successful. Despite the challenging conditions, Ship arrived off the shores of Australia's Christmas Island in August.

Once in the calmer Christmas waters, SpaceX engineers took time to perform a vehicle inspection and collect a number of heat shield samples from the spacecraft's belly. From there, Ship 40 was loaded onto "Forte," a massive, semi-submersible transport ship for the long seaward journey back to Texas.

Forte arrived at the Port of Brownsville on Oct. 7, wrapping up the longest stretch of Ship 40's return nearly two months after its liftoff. The spacecraft was subsequently transported over land back to Starbase and positioned for reorientation outside the Megabay. It has since been lifted to a vertical position and moved inside the bay alongside three other Ship upper stages still under assembly.

While SpaceX has successfully recovered a trio of Super Heavy boosters using the mechanical arms of its Starbase launch tower, the company has yet to return a Starship upper stage to its launch site under its own power. The return of Ship 40 will give SpaceX engineers the opportunity to study the vehicle from top to bottom as they fine-tune the systems needed to do just that. Its return marks a milestone in SpaceX's efforts to develop Starship as a rapidly reusable launch vehicle, with lessons from the recovered spacecraft potentially informing future vehicle designs and recovery operations.

Ship 40's immediate successor, Ship 41, launched on Flight 14 before 40's return to Starbase. Although 41 didn't survive its splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, the mission marked Starship's first orbital flight, and included the successful deployment of 26 next-generation Starlink V3 satellites.

Musk has said Starship's next launch, Flight 15, could feature the first attempt to catch the Ship upper stage using the same chopstick-like arms on the vehicle's launch tower, provided the spacecraft meets the necessary conditions for a safe return. SpaceX has not announced an official launch date for Starship's next flight, but, based on the testing progress of the Ship and Super Heavy in line for the mission, it is likely to fly within the next month or so.

]]> <![CDATA[ Four years ago, NASA punched an asteroid. Europe's Hera probe arrives this month to inspect the wreckage ]]> NASA's DART mission made a cosmic mess four years ago — and now a new spacecraft is ready to scout out exactly what the first-of-its-kind collision accomplished.

The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft slammed into a small space rock called Dimorphos on Sept. 26, 2022, in humanity's first test of planetary defense. That's the field dedicated to protecting Earth from the possibility of a calamitous asteroid impact, and DART mimicked how humans could change the orbit of a threatening space rock, taking it off its collision course.

The mission definitely succeeded, shortening the little asteroid's orbit around a larger rock called Didymos by about 33 minutes. But in order to make the most of the experiment, scientists ensured a second spacecraft would follow DART at a more leisurely pace. That decision will pay off this month with the arrival of a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft dubbed Hera, which launched in October 2024, two years after DART's impact.

"Hera wants to be the detective, like Inspector Colombo, going back to the crash scene," said Patrick Michel, a planetary scientist at the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) and principal investigator of the Hera mission.

Scientists have been able to do limited monitoring of the Didymos system over the years with telescopes both on the ground and in space. That's how they calculated the basic change to the orbit, and they've built a basic sketch of what happened.

"We know that there was a lot of material kicked up," said Angela Stickle, a planetary scientist at Johns Hopkins University's Applied Physics Laboratory affiliated with both missions. "We know that we probably left a pretty significant mark on Dimorphos."

But the story isn't over and scientists are far from satisfied. No one knows how big a crater the impact left, or whether it completely rearranged all the asteroid's boulders. There are hints Dimorphos is now tumbling, and material may have moved between it and the larger Didymos.

Even the change to the orbit is complicated, said Cristina Thomas, a planetary astronomer at Northern Arizona University affiliated with both missions: The time Dimorphos took to circle Didymos was still changing some six months after impact, for reasons that aren't clear. "This thing that we thought was going to be very cut and dry turned out to be really interesting and complicated," Thomas said.

That's where Hera comes in, with its first arrival maneuver scheduled for Oct. 15. During three careful braking maneuvers, the spacecraft will slow down and approach the space rocks. Assuming everything goes smoothly, by early November, the spacecraft will come within 20 miles (30 kilometers) of the two rocks and begin its early science observations, then move even closer in early December.

Mission personnel can't wait for their first glimpses of Dimorphos — the first time scientists will visit someplace they've seen before without knowing what they'll find. "For us, it's like a new world," Michel said. "The new image won't have anything to do with the previous one, so that's really exciting."

In addition to mapping the two asteroids and seeing what kind of crater the impact left, scientists will also have their eyes peeled for any pieces of the DART spacecraft, although they don't expect to find anything. "We were coming in really fast, so typically, the whole spacecraft you would expect to just kind of shatter or melt," Stickle said. The only sliver of possibility is that part of the two long solar panels stretching off the spacecraft may have snapped off and survived. (The appendages may also have turned the crater shape into an oval.)

In January, once Hera has settled in, it will release two tiny companions that have piggybacked out to Dimorphos. One, called Milani, will identify the composition of materials on and around Dimorphos. The other, Juventas, will use radar to peer inside Dimorphos — the first time scientists have ever been able to study the interior of a space rock directly. Juventas will end its mission by landing on the small asteroid, and Milani may attempt a landing as well.

The trio of spacecraft will operate in tandem throughout early 2027, and the main spacecraft will operate at least through September 2027. All told, they will give scientists an unprecedented look at the pair of asteroids — the first binary asteroid a spacecraft has ever studied in detail. And the Didymos–Dimorphos duo is a good one to visit first. "It's very ordinary, and I mean that in the best possible way," Thomas said.

Ordinary except, of course, for that time humans punched it, opening the door for the Hera mission to explore the previously unremarkable rocks. And finally, that moment is just around the corner.

"Nothing really worries me," Michel said of the spacecraft's arrival. "It's really just excitement now."

On Oct. 13, 1773, a French astronomer named Charles Messier discovered the "Whirlpool Galaxy," also known as Messier 51, or M51.

Charles Messier was scanning the sky for objects that could confuse comet hunters when he catalogued the galaxy as M51. However, Messier wasn't able to see the spiral structure, and he didn't identify it as a galaxy.

Seventy-two years later, another astronomer named William Parsons saw the whirlpool shape, but he thought it was a spiral nebula. Eventually, Edwin Hubble found out that M51 and other features like it were actually galaxies.

Why it mattered

The Whirlpool Galaxy is located about 31 million light-years from Earth and just might be the textbook case of a spiral galaxy. But in 1773, it was just one of 51 (at the time of its discovery) of "comet-like 'objects to avoid'" in the night sky.

The Whirlpool Galaxy's designation as M51 marks it as the 51st non-comet object catalogued by Messier, who was the chief astronomer of the Marine Observatory in Paris dedicated to studying comets. According to a NASA account, Messier stumbled across his first non-comet object, M1 (also known as the Crab Nebula), while studying a comet in 1758. The objects looked like fuzzy blobs like comets, but didn't move like a comet. By 1773, at the time he first spotted M51, he had catalogued over four dozen such objects to help prevent astronomers from mistaking them for comets.

The Whirlpool Galaxy appears as a dazzling spiral in images by the Hubble Space Telescope, and has a magnitude of 8.4 on the brightness scale used by astronomers. That means it can be observed through a small telescope ("most easily during May," NASA says) in the constellation Venatici (the Hunting Dogs) in the northern sky, just below the handle of the Big Dipper star pattern.

Scientists suspsect the Whirpool Galaxy gets is striking spiral shape from a close interaction with its neighbor galaxy NGC 5195, which may have passed through M51's main disk about 500 million years ago, scientists with NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope have said.

"This gravitational tug of war may also have triggered an increased level of star formation in M51," they added in a statement. "The companion galaxy's pull would be inducing extra starbirth by compressing gas, jump-starting the process by which stars form."

"The Star Trek Tour made the most sense, so I worked with Space Center to relocate it, and it arrived a couple of years ago."

Hoping to give the restored relic its own private docking bay due to its enormity, faithful fans raised hundreds of thousands of dollars via a Kickstarter campaign led by Brian Mix and David Harvey, and built a beautiful building addition for Galileo to be safely ensconced in.

"My wife Leslie and I had been tending over the Galileo for a number of years, and it's now successfully displayed there in New York for all to see," Schneider adds. Such a shift can affect climate, both on local scales and globally, as regions that were by the poles find themselves moving down to lower latitudes and vice versa. This can then affect atmospheric circulation patterns, which affect climate across the world.

"You can imagine my surprise when I opened my back door to let the dogs out this morning," Ellen Alence told Space.com. She snapped a pic of the rocket from her farm Colbert, Georgia.

"Many of you are talking about the 'space jellyfish' following this morning's launch from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida," NASA's Kennedy Space Center wrote in a post on X. The post explains the "jellyfish" phenomenon that is sometimes visible during dawn and dusk launches, and included additional photos of the launch.

"A jellyfish happens near sunrise or sunset when the exhaust plume from the rocket becomes brightly illuminated, creating a glowing shape resembling a jellyfish," the post said.

Further up the coast, Richard Mack Wilson-Leigh spotted the flight from Durham, North Carolina. His view of the rocket came just seconds before the vehicle's stage separation, which was followed immediately by the rocket's main booster performing an engine burn to right its trajectory for landing back at the Cape. Wilson-Leigh said that part caught him off guard more than the initial site of the rocket. "I thought it blew up at first," he jokingly told Space.com.

"At first, I thought it was a comet," Wilson-Leigh said. "My mind jumped between two thoughts: that is just beautiful beyond belief, and it is the end of the world.”

That stage separation came about 2.5 minutes after liftoff, and put on a dazzling display for those awake to see it this morning. As Falcon 9's booster began the journey to its landing zone, the rocket's second stage continued onward to orbit with Dragon and the capsule's 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of cargo for the ISS.

The spacecraft will spend roughly two days catching up to the ISS, where a recent personnel rotation swapped the astronauts of SpaceX's Crew-12 mission with those of Crew-13. The latter arrived aboard the orbital laboratory Oct. 1, which was followed several days later by the return of Crew-12 to Earth on Oct. 8.

The Dragon carrying the contents of CRS-35's manifest will arrive at the station Thursday morning (Oct. 15), and will autonomously dock to the space-facing port of the Harmony module at around 11 a.m. EDT (1500 GMT). Coverage of the arrival here at Space.com beginning at 9:15 a.m. EDT (1315 GMT).

]]> <![CDATA[ 2 spacecraft in orbit and 8 more coming soon: Varda has big plans for in-space manufacturing ]]> Reentry and orbital-manufacturing provider Varda Space Industries is operating two spacecraft in orbit right now, with another expected to launch "in the coming days" and seven more next year.

The Los Angeles-area startup, which bills itself as one of just two companies that can currently do commercial reentry from space, successfully launched its latest two refrigerator-sized spacecraft aboard SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission on Oct. 1.

"It's humanity's first time launching multiple commercial reentry vehicles simultaneously," Varda CEO Will Bruey told Space.com on Tuesday (Oct. 7) of the Transporter-18 launch.

The payloads on the Transporter-18 Varda craft ranged from pharmaceuticals to demo navigation systems to exterior thermal-protection materials. The company bills its spacecraft as mini-factories, which can host the orbital production of valuable goods such as pharmaceuticals and then bring them safely down to Earth.

Another Varda vehicle is scheduled to follow them into space later this month. Assuming the third spacecraft launches nominally, all three will come down before Christmas in the Koonibba Test Range in the South Australian Outback, through coordination with Varda's long-time space-mission service provider, Southern Launch. And things are scheduled to ramp up quickly: Varda aims to fly seven more missions in 2027: two in Quarter 1 (Q1), two in Q2 and three in Q3 (the latter three being all on the same rocket).

"As we scale up, we care about our ability to fly and fly regularly," Bruey said, emphasizing that the company is now treating its missions less as one-offs and more as a series. "It is, first and foremost, taking that unique [spacecraft] technology and moving into a fleet mentality, rather than a space mission mentality."

Like any startup finding its footing, Varda's challenges in the coming months will be scaling safely and efficiently. But the company says it is well-capitalized to do so, and has a big hiring campaign underway. It also has been spending money on slight upgrades and improvements to its vehicles, as well as mission operations and other infrastructure to run several missions at the same time, with more funds having just arrived.

In September, Varda announced it had raised $251 million in "Series D" investment funding and will be hiring 100 people by the end of 2027, boosting its current 286-employee base by more than a third. Most of the employees work out of El Segundo, California, with a few in sales offices in Washington, D.C. and Huntsville, Alabama (where U.S. Space Command is gradually moving, along with some defense contractors, from Colorado Springs).

In the further future, Bruey said, the goal is to fly Varda vehicles into space daily, using a "standardized product" that would be put together on an assembly line. But to get to that point, like other companies in the industry, Varda will need to get through an anticipated rocket shortage beginning in about 2029.

SpaceX is by far the most active launcher these days, and it has been the dominant provider for companies like Varda via its Transporter and Bandwagon rideshare programs. But SpaceX is readying to retire its Falcon 9 rocket as it transitions more resources into Starship, the fully reusable megarocket the company sees as its workhorse of the future. Media reports suggest that SpaceX is pretty much out of capacity for Falcon 9 rockets flying through the end of service in 2028 or 2029, although slots are still available through third-party bookers.

"We're stacked with launches from now through that 2029 time frame," Bruey said. The company's current generation of vehicles is "launch-agnostic," although the next generation is aiming to be even more so to nab opportunities from small rockets up to Starship.

The company said that, as long as Varda and its customers have access to microgravity, the shipping methodology — much like shipping on Earth — should not matter, and Varda aims to make the experience that seamless for its customers. SpaceX is by far the most active launcher these days, and it has been the dominant provider for companies like Varda via its Transporter and Bandwagon rideshare programs. But SpaceX is readying to retire its Falcon 9 rocket as it transitions more resources into Starship, the fully reusable megarocket the company sees as its workhorse of the future. Media reports suggest that SpaceX is pretty much out of capacity for Falcon 9 rockets flying through the end of service in 2028 or 2029, although slots are still available through third-party bookers.

There are a slew of newer rockets under production (such as Blue Origin's New Glenn and Relativity Space's Terran R), though they are far less mature and in some cases, even unflown. This is creating uncertainty about how much capacity there will be in the industry in the short term, but Varda said it is planning well ahead for that moment — and so too are its customers.

"We're stacked with launches from now through that 2029 time frame," Bruey said. The company's current generation of vehicles is "launch-agnostic," although the next generation is aiming to be even more so to nab opportunities from small rockets up to Starship.

The company said that, as long as Varda and its customers have access to microgravity, the shipping methodology — much like shipping on Earth — should not matter, and Varda aims to make the experience that seamless for its customers. But in the meantime, the company says it will fly as much as possible and (like everyone else) do what it can to secure slots on launching rockets after Falcon 9 retires.

<description>Český T-Mobile nasadil na zákaznickou infolinku hlasového AI asistenta, který dokáže odpovídat na běžné dotazy k vyúčtování, roamingu nebo službám operátora. Česká pobočka má vedoucí roli v projektu, který chce mateřská Deutsche Telekom rozvíjet i v dal&#353;ích zemích. Technologii navíc dodává ceněný startup, kde mají podíl i Če&#353;i.</description>

výběžek.eu https://www.vybezek.eu dobrý den ze šluknovského výběžku, konce světa - šluknovský výběžek Tue, 13 Oct 2026 07:49:21 +0000 cs hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 https://www.vybezek.eu/wp-uploads/2018/09/cropped-favicon-vybezek-32x32.png výběžek.eu https://www.vybezek.eu 32 32 Horní Podluží – slavnostní předání zásahového vozidla JSDH https://www.vybezek.eu/295716-horni-podluzi-slavnostni-predani-zasahoveho-vozidla-jsdh/ Sat, 10 Oct 2026 14:52:31 +0000 https://www.vybezek.eu/?p=295716 V sobotu 10. října 2026 pod sjezdovkou v Horním Podluží proběhlo slavnostní předání zásahového vozidla místní JSDH.

Za účasti hostů a dalších hasičských jednotek proběhlo slavnostní převzetí automobilu IVECO, který připutoval z Prahy. Dosavadní Tatra se přesune do služby do Národního parku České Švýcarsko.

Že je hasičů stále třeba a že mají práce víc než dost dokazovaly průběžné výjezdy k nedaleké havárii osobního auta u Jiřetína pod Jedlovou či do Varnsdorfu k srnce v korytě Mandavy.

Na technické podrobnosti počkáme na odborníky.

Požáry.cz:

Vozidlo, které dosud sloužilo u Hasičského záchranného sboru hlavního města Prahy, nyní zamířilo k Hasiči Horní Podluží , kde po nezbytných úpravách a doplnění vlastního vybavení posílilo akceschopnost místních dobrovolných hasičů.

Podrobně:

Hasiči v Horním Podluží posilují vozový park, z Prahy získali cisternový speciál Iveco Trakker.

Jednotka sboru dobrovolných hasičů obce Horní Podluží (JPO III) se dočkala významné posily v podobě speciálního požárního automobilu Iveco Trakker AD3.

Vozidlo, které dosud sloužilo u Hasičského záchranného sboru hlavního města Prahy, nyní zamířilo do severočeské obce, kde po nezbytných úpravách a doplnění vlastního vybavení posílilo akceschopnost místních dobrovolných hasičů.

Slavnostní předání cisterny hornopodlužské dobrovolné jednotce proběhlo 10. října 2026 za účasti mnoha kolegů z okolních obcí, dorazili i kolegové z Německa. Nechyběli ani zástupci HZS Ústeckého kraje a HZS Praha – kpt. Ing. Jan Matějovský a kpt. Bc. Jaromír Laštůvka z pracoviště strojní služby.

Cisternový automobil na podvozku Iveco Trakker byl vyroben v roce 2010 a na svém tachometru eviduje 45 654 ujetých kilometrů. Ačkoliv se pro pražský HZS stal nadbytečným majetkem, jeho technický stav je plně pojízdný, odpovídající stáří a s platnou STK.

Původní pořizovací hodnota samotného vozidla dosahovala 8 000 478 Kč. Bezúplatný převod majetku ve veřejném zájmu schválilo zastupitelstvo obce Horní Podluží usnesením v červnu 2026.

Když na předání mířila dolnopodlužská jednotka, narazila jen pár set metrů od sjezdovky na dopravní nehodu osobního vozidla. Provedla zabezpečení místa a po zjištění, že zasahovat už není na místě třeba, odjela původně zamýšleným směrem.

Nicméně chvíli poté byla ke stejné nehodě operačním střediskem vyslána profesionální jednotka z Varnsdorfu společně s kolegy z Horního Podluží, část jednotky tak urychleně opustila místo slavnostního předání a vyjela k nehodě.

Za dalších pár minut na plac u sjezdovky dorazila i dobrovolná jednotka z Varnsdorfu, která se ale vzápětí otočila a jela zpět do města, zachránit srnce z řeky.

Až po této šachové partii a návratu hornopodlužské jednotky na místo mohlo slavnostní předání konečně proběhnout.
